Q7343.t: Turquoise lace stitched along Australia's coast
Q7343.s: Look for patches of turquoise and pale lace scattered over deep navy water, far off the Queensland coast. Each is a reef built by living coral, and together they form the largest coral reef system on Earth, running for about 2,300 km. It is so big that astronauts can pick it out from orbit.
Q7343.w: Turquoise and cream patches on dark blue sea, well offshore, lined up parallel to the Queensland coast.
f: It is made up of roughly 3,000 separate reefs and about 900 islands.
UNESCO listed the reef as a World Heritage site in 1981.
Once a year, a few nights after a full moon in October or November, its corals release their eggs almost all at once.

q.q: Roughly how long is the Great Barrier Reef?

Q118841.t: A mile-deep gash with Earth's history on its walls
Q118841.s: Even from 11 km up the Grand Canyon looks like a wound in the plateau: a jagged chasm of red, orange and cream layers, with the Colorado River a thin green-brown thread at the bottom. It is about 446 km long and up to 29 km wide. In places the river runs some 1,800 metres below the rim.
Q118841.w: A branching maze of red and cream cliffs cutting the flat plateau, the river hidden deep inside.
f: The oldest rocks at the bottom of the canyon are nearly two billion years old.
The North Rim is about 300 m higher than the South Rim, gets far more snow and closes to visitors in winter.
The Grand Canyon became a US national park in 1919.

q.q: Which river carved the Grand Canyon?

Q43278.t: A waterfall that announces itself with a cloud
Q43278.s: Before you see the falls you may see their cloud: a white plume of spray rising above the Zambezi, visible from dozens of kilometres away when the river is high. Below it the water drops into a narrow chasm about 1.7 km long, then zigzags through a chain of gorges. Locally it is called Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the smoke that thunders'.
Q43278.w: A white mist above the Zambezi, then a sharp zigzag of gorges below it, on the Zambia–Zimbabwe border.
f: About 1,700 m wide and over 100 m high, it is one of the largest sheets of falling water in the world.
David Livingstone reached the falls in 1855 and named them after Queen Victoria.
The zigzag gorges downstream are former lips of the falls, left behind as the water cut its way back upstream.

q.q: What does the local name Mosi-oa-Tunya mean?

Q34221.t: Where Lake Erie spills over a cliff towards Ontario
Q34221.s: From the air, look for a white smudge of spray between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario: that is the Horseshoe Falls, curved just like its name. The Niagara River carries the outflow of four Great Lakes over the edge of the Niagara Escarpment here. The falls formed roughly 12,000 years ago, as the ice sheets melted back.
Q34221.w: A short river linking Lake Erie and Lake Ontario; the falls are a white patch where it bends.
f: There are three falls: the big Horseshoe Falls on the Canadian side, and the American and Bridal Veil Falls next door.
The falls are about 50 m high; creeping upstream, they have cut a gorge some 11 km long.
At night much of the river is diverted to hydroelectric plants, so less water goes over the falls.

q.q: Which two lakes does the Niagara River connect?

Q36332.t: Some 275 falls strung along one jungle cliff
Q36332.s: Iguaçu is not one waterfall but a whole horseshoe of them: around 275 separate cascades spread along nearly 3 km of cliff, on the border of Brazil and Argentina. From above, look for a brown river breaking into white foam inside green forest. The deepest point, the U-shaped Devil's Throat, swallows about half of the river's flow.
Q36332.w: White foam in green forest, just east of where the Iguaçu River meets the wide Paraná.
f: The river's name comes from the Guarani words for 'big water'.
Both the Argentine and the Brazilian national parks around the falls are UNESCO World Heritage sites.
Downstream the Iguaçu joins the Paraná at a point where Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay meet.

q.q: Which two countries share Iguaçu Falls?

Q3783.t: A café-au-lait river in an ocean of green
Q3783.s: Below you the Amazon, here still called the Solimões, is a broad café-au-lait band wandering through unbroken green, with side channels, islands and lakes along both banks. It carries about a fifth of all the river water that reaches the world's oceans. Not a single bridge crosses its main stream.
Q3783.w: A wide brown river with pale sandbars and dark lakes on either side, cutting through unbroken forest.
f: Its average flow is around 200,000 cubic metres per second, more than the next several largest rivers combined.
At Manaus the dark Rio Negro joins it, and the two waters run side by side for kilometres before mixing.
In 1500 Vicente Yáñez Pinzón found fresh water at sea off its mouth and named the river the 'Sweet Sea'.

q.q: What is the Amazon called in Brazil above Manaus?

Q3392.t: A green thread stitched through the Sahara
Q3392.s: Few sights from the air are as stark as this: a single blue-green line with a narrow fringe of fields and palms, and bare desert on both sides. Here in northern Sudan the Nile makes its Great Bend, flowing south-west for a few hundred kilometres before turning north again. Nubian kings built pyramids along this stretch.
Q3392.w: A thin dark line with a green fringe across pale desert, curving in a big S.
f: At about 6,650 km, the Nile is one of the two longest rivers on Earth, alongside the Amazon.
Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt, around two hundred of them, smaller and steeper than Giza's.
Its water comes from two sources: the White Nile from the lakes of East Africa and the Blue Nile from Ethiopia.

q.q: Where do the White Nile and the Blue Nile meet?

Q932289.t: Africa's great green heart, cut by brown rivers
Q932289.s: For hundreds of kilometres there is almost nothing but forest: a dense green carpet, cut by brown rivers that loop and braid through it. This is the heart of the Congo basin, home to the second-largest tropical rainforest on Earth after the Amazon. By afternoon towering thunderclouds often build over it, fed by moisture the trees themselves breathe out.
Q932289.w: Unbroken dark green forest with meandering brown rivers; in the afternoon, clusters of tall white storm clouds.
f: The Congo River crosses the equator twice as it curves round the basin.
Bonobos live only here, south of the Congo River.
In 2017 scientists mapped a huge peatland beneath its swamp forests, the largest tropical peatland known.

q.q: Which ape lives only south of the Congo River?

Q244451.t: The greatest river basin on Earth, roofed in forest
Q244451.s: Look down and count the shades of green: canopy, swamp forest, pale patches of grassland, and rivers the colour of tea or milky coffee. This is the Amazon lowland, where forest still runs to the horizon in most directions. In places, straight roads with side tracks cut into it in a fishbone pattern, the mark of clearing for farms.
Q244451.w: Endless forest crossed by winding rivers; near roads, rectangular clearings arranged like a fishbone.
f: The Amazon's drainage basin covers about 7 million km², the largest of any river on Earth.
Much of the rain here was first evaporated by the forest itself, recycled again and again as air moves west.
Dust blown across the Atlantic from the Sahara helps fertilise the forest's poor soils.

q.q: Where does much of the dust that fertilises the Amazon come from?

Q797.t: America's biggest state, and its emptiest
Q797.s: Below you is the Alaskan interior: dark spruce forest, a glitter of lakes and the wide braided channels of the Yukon and its tributaries, with hardly a road in sight. Alaska is more than twice the size of Texas. On a clear day the white bulk of Denali, North America's highest peak at 6,190 m, may stand out far to the south.
Q797.w: Dark forest, silvery lakes and braided rivers with almost no roads; snowy ranges on the southern horizon.
f: The United States bought Alaska from Russia in 1867 for 7.2 million dollars.
Alaska has a longer coastline than all the other US states combined.
In Fairbanks, in the interior, midsummer days last almost 22 hours.

q.q: From which country did the US buy Alaska in 1867?

Q5428.t: Taiga from horizon to horizon, for hours on end
Q5428.s: You can fly for hours over Siberia and see little but taiga: dark larch and pine forest, winding rivers and, in winter, snow that turns the whole land white and blue. Here, on the Central Siberian Plateau, the Lena, the Lower Tunguska and their tributaries cut deep valleys. Siberia covers roughly three-quarters of Russia.
Q5428.w: Endless dark forest and looping rivers in deep valleys; in winter, white snow with grey larch woods showing through.
f: Siberia covers about 13 million km², more than Canada or China.
Much of the taiga here is larch, which sheds its needles, so in winter the forest looks grey rather than green.
Lake Baikal, in southern Siberia, holds about a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water.

q.q: Which Siberian lake is the deepest on Earth?

Q866405.t: The bigger, older half of Antarctica's ice
Q866405.s: If you ever see this, it will be a white emptiness without edges: the East Antarctic ice sheet, more than 4 km thick in places and rising to over 4,000 m. Near here stands Russia's Vostok Station, where −89.2 °C was recorded in 1983, the lowest air temperature ever measured by a weather station.
Q866405.w: Flat white ice to every horizon, with no landmarks at all; blinding in the summer sun.
f: About 4 km beneath Vostok Station lies Lake Vostok, a body of liquid water sealed under the ice.
The East Antarctic ice sheet holds enough water to raise world sea level by more than 50 metres.
This ice sheet has been building up for more than 30 million years.

q.q: What lies about 4 km beneath Vostok Station?

Q530917.t: An ice sheet resting on a floor below the sea
Q530917.s: West Antarctica looks like its eastern twin from above, white, silent and endless, but beneath the ice it is very different. Much of its bedrock lies far below sea level, so the ice sheet rests in a deep basin that the ocean could reach. Scientists watch its glaciers closely, because they are among the fastest-changing on Earth.
Q530917.w: An unbroken white plain; towards the coast, dark mountain ridges and crevassed glaciers break through the ice.
f: Vinson Massif, Antarctica's highest peak at 4,892 m, rises in West Antarctica's Ellsworth Mountains.
If all its ice melted, world sea level would rise by several metres.
The Transantarctic Mountains separate it from East Antarctica.

Q76034.t: Billions of years old, and speckled with lakes
Q76034.s: From the air the Canadian Shield looks as if someone had shattered a mirror over the land: thousands of lakes of every shape, bare pink-grey rock and dark patches of spruce or open tundra, all scraped and polished by ice-age glaciers. This is the ancient core of North America. Some of its rocks formed when Earth was barely half a billion years old.
Q76034.w: A jigsaw of countless lakes and bare rock with streaks of forest; in winter, white lakes framed by dark trees.
f: The shield covers roughly half of Canada, wrapped around Hudson Bay like a horseshoe.
The Acasta Gneiss in the Northwest Territories, about 4 billion years old, is among the oldest known rocks on Earth.
Its rocks hold rich deposits of nickel, gold, copper and diamonds.

q.q: Which bay does the Canadian Shield wrap around?

Q147304.t: Land built grain by grain by the Yellow River
Q147304.s: Below spreads one of the flattest and most crowded farmlands on Earth: a fine mosaic of fields, villages scattered like grains of rice, and often a grey-brown haze over it all. Most of the plain was laid down as silt by the Yellow River, which has shifted its course across it many times. In June, ripe winter wheat turns it gold.
Q147304.w: A vast flat patchwork of small fields and villages, often under haze; green in spring, gold in early summer.
f: The Grand Canal, the longest artificial waterway in the world, crosses the plain between Beijing and Hangzhou.
In places the Yellow River flows higher than the fields around it, held between tall levees.
Around 1855 the Yellow River moved its mouth from south of the Shandong Peninsula to north of it.

q.q: Which river laid down most of the North China Plain?

Q602925.t: Grassland to every horizon, in the heart of Eurasia
Q602925.s: Here the land opens up completely: rolling grassland, green in May and straw-gold by midsummer, crossed by dirt tracks and dotted with salt lakes that flash white in the sun. The huge rectangular fields in the north date from the Soviet Virgin Lands campaign of the 1950s. In winter everything is white and scoured by wind.
Q602925.w: Flat to rolling tan grassland, straight dirt tracks, white salt pans and huge rectangular fields further north.
f: In the Virgin Lands campaign, begun in 1954, millions of hectares of Kazakh steppe were ploughed for wheat.
The lakes of Korgalzhyn, west of Astana, hold one of the world's most northerly flamingo colonies.
Saiga antelope, with their swollen, trunk-like noses, still roam the Kazakh steppe.

q.q: Which antelope with a trunk-like nose roams the Kazakh Steppe?

Q560549.t: Flat land from the North Sea all the way to the Urals
Q560549.s: You are over the north-eastern end of Europe's great lowland, which runs from the North Sea through Germany and Poland and across Russia to the Urals. Out here it is taiga and bog: dark forest, brown peatland glinting with pools, and rivers like the Pechora wandering in broad loops. In the west the same plain is a quilt of fields and towns.
Q560549.w: Dark taiga, brown bogs with glinting pools and looping rivers, stretching flat to the horizon.
f: On average the plain lies less than 200 m above sea level.
Its gentle hills and chains of lakes in Germany and Poland are moraines left by Ice Age glaciers.
The Pechora, which drains its north-eastern part, flows into the Barents Sea.

q.q: Which mountains mark the plain's eastern end?

Q12707.t: Where the land is ruled into squares a mile wide
Q12707.s: Look for the grid: roads a mile apart, square fields in green, gold and brown, and here and there perfect circles where pivot sprinklers water the crops. The Great Plains roll from Canada to Texas, east of the Rockies. Once shortgrass prairie grazed by tens of millions of bison, they are now one of the great grain belts of the world.
Q12707.w: A ruler-straight grid of roads and fields; to the west, the crumpled badlands of the Little Missouri River.
f: Much of the southern Plains is watered from the Ogallala Aquifer, one of the largest aquifers in the world.
The mile-square grid goes back to the Land Ordinance of 1785, which set out how US land was surveyed.
The Plains tilt gently east, losing well over a kilometre of height from the foot of the Rockies.

q.q: Why do many fields on the Great Plains look like perfect circles?
